subject: knight
pitch: A fantasy knight in battle-worn plate armour. A great helm with a narrow eye slit and a tall crimson plume, layered shoulder plates etched with gold filigree, a deep-blue surcoat with a silver griffin emblem, a tall kite shield bearing the same griffin, and a broadsword. Dents and scratches tell of many battles, and a torn crimson cape hangs from the shoulders.
reasoning:
I'm planning a single TypeScript module building a humanoid knight using the SDK — a standing rest pose with named joints, bone chains, paints, and textured geometry with UVs for details like the griffin emblem, making sure everything matches the API correctly.

Reviewing the key API surface I'll rely on: joints, chains with paths and named sub-joints, sweeps and lofts for limbs and torso, parts for placed geometry, extrude/lathe for flat and rotational shapes, and surface/ring helpers for distributing details across the mesh.

Now I'm sketching the actual knight build: setting up coordinate conventions (Y up, +Z forward, +X left), targeting roughly 1.9m height, and planning the skeleton starting with a pelvis joint around y=1.0 as the root of the spine chain.

I'm working through chain parenting logic—building a spine chain from pelvis through chest to neck, figuring out how span counts and names map to the joint path, and making sure the chain's first joint correctly attaches to the existing pelvis via nearest-joint weighting.

With names length 3 the tip joint lands correctly at the span end. Then I add a "head" joint above neck, and plan the great helm geometry as a lathed or lofted box shape over the head.

For simpler blocky parts I'll fall back to using three.js primitive geometries (boxes, cylinders, spheres) through a part helper with color and positioning, reserving painted nested surfaces for gold filigree or dents where it adds value without over-engineering.

I'm picking out a palette: brushed steel with grain/mottle paints for grime, crimson, deep blue, gold, and silver, all baked into textures so they're cheap. For dents and scratches I'm planning a custom paint function using cell noise to darken small patches rather than adding extra geometry.

Adding dent texture...

For the griffin emblem, I'm thinking of using an SVG silhouette texture on a plane geometry placed over the surcoat front, tinting it a pale silver-grey so it reads as a griffin crest rather than trying to paint it procedurally.

For the shield, I'll place the same textured plane on the shield's front face, positioned slightly offset so it sits atop the extruded kite shape without clipping.

That gives a front face in the XY plane facing +Z, positioned at chest level on the left. For placing the griffin plane, I'm figuring out how to use the shield's frame so the plane's local +Z axis lines up with the shield's own outward normal, using the extrude part's orientation basis to drive the frame option.

Now I'm working out joint placement for the arms and shield/sword positions — shield on the knight's left arm (+X side), sword in the right hand (-X side), with a shoulder-elbow-wrist chain parented to the chest/spine, defining approximate joint coordinates for a natural resting arm pose.

Moving to the legs, I'm laying out hip-knee-ankle chains parented to the hips, with coordinates descending from hip to ankle, and planning sabaton-style feet for the armor.

For the head, I'm placing a joint above the neck tip, parented to the neck, relying on default parent-quaternion alignment since no explicit direction is needed there. For the plume, I'm sweeping a curved path from the helm top upward and backward with tapering radius to create the crimson crest.

Settling on a tapered radius array like [0.035, 0.012, 0.002] for keyed linear interpolation along the rod, which works fine either way for the plume shape. Planning the plume itself as a tube sweep along the path.

For the great helm, I'm sketching a loft defined by stations from crown to chin, with the head centered around (0,1.66,0) and helm stations spanning y 1.5 to 1.85 with varying widths.

Now I'm working out the eye slit — a dark narrow box placed on the helm's front face to read as a visor opening, needing to figure out the correct z-offset where the loft surface actually sits.

Working out the frame orientation without an explicit up vector: for an upward path along Y, I'm tracing through the default aim/basis construction to figure out whether the normal ends up as +Z or -Z, which determines how the binormal falls out from the cross product of tangent and normal.

So for ring vertices I settle on width (x-scale) tracking the binormal direction, and depth (y-scale) tracking the normal -- meaning for the helm's vertical loft, width aligns with X and depth with Z. I'll set station depths at each height level, keep the loft centered at the origin, and go with THREE.js loft geometry rather than a scaled sphere for a more blocky, deliberate helm shape, adding features like a T-slit visor and crest on top.

Now I'm adding a plume on the crown, binding the helm to the head joint, and sketching a neck gorget as a simple cylinder attached to the neck bone. For the torso I'm defining loft stations along the spine chain from hips to upper chest, specifying width/height at each height to shape the pelvis, waist, and chest before working out how the catmull path threads through those points.

A deep blue surcoat lofts slightly larger over the torso, flaring at the hem near the hips while the steel cuirass shows through at the chest. I'm positioning a griffin emblem plane on the surcoat's front face, estimating its z-offset and size based on the surcoat's thickness around the chest height.

I realize I should instead use a surface-nearest query to find a hit point and attach the emblem there, but the stick function aims the plane's local +Y along the surface normal, while my plane geometry's natural normal faces +Z — meaning it would lie flat and tangent instead of facing outward. I need to rotate the geometry so it's properly oriented before sticking it to the surface.

I'll avoid the flush-to-surface approach and instead place the geometry slightly offset along the normal using a small lift, orienting a flat quad so its face aligns with the hit normal via a quaternion that rotates +Z to match.

I'll set the position slightly offset along the normal to avoid z-fighting, pass in the computed quaternion directly, and let weights derive from the position point rather than a separate frame.

Surcoat needs to be built before parts since loft returns a Sweep that surface() can accept directly. For the griffin's nearest-point lookup, I'm checking that a point like [0,1.05,0.5] correctly resolves to the front position.

I'll handle the shield's griffin placement the same way via local extrude. For the torn crimson cape, I'm defining a membrane stretched between two polyline edges—a shoulder line and a hemline—with tearing effects added through additional geometry to give it that ragged look.

I need to position the cape behind the torso, so I'll set edge A's z-coordinate to sit just clear of the torso's back depth, keeping the shoulder width around 0.42. With a bone specified, the membrane's edge weights will resolve to a rigid binding on that joint rather than blending smoothly.

For the shoulder pauldrons, I'm designing layered dome-shaped plates using lathe geometry with a bowl-like profile, attached at the shoulder joint and sized to fit the arm chain's first bone.

For the gold filigree accents, I'm painting thin horizontal gold stripe bands onto the pauldron surface using a stripes pattern along the vertical axis.

Now I'm adding dents and scratches to the steel surface using a cell-based noise pattern, where thin lines along cell borders get darkened to simulate scratch marks, which I'll combine with the base steel paint.

I should cache the cell lookup to avoid redundant computation since the grid will be evaluated at high resolution. Now I'm moving on to outlining a kite-shaped shield for the left arm, defining its vertices in a local XY plane centered at the shield's origin.

Still placing shield geometry...

For the shield face, I'm thinking deep blue with a mottled texture, maybe steel rim trim, positioned so the boss sits slightly forward of the front plane.

Now I'm working out the shield's attachment bone, likely the left wrist, and checking the arm chain positions from shoulder to elbow to wrist line up so the shield sits naturally against the forearm. For the sword, I'm placing it in the right hand at the wrist joint.

Writing sword blade geometry...

Placing the grip, pommel, and blade base at the hilt attached to wristR, then setting up the leg chains with hip, knee, and ankle joints positioned symmetrically down each side from the hips.

Now I'm sweeping a tapered radius along each leg chain to build the greaves, then adding sabaton boxes at the ankle bones for the feet.

For arms, I'll sweep the arm chain similarly for vambrace/couter coverage, with simple sphere or box shapes at the wrist for hands. For the torso, I'm lofting the spine into a steel cuirass and layering a wider blue surcoat loft lower down to resemble a tabard draped over the plate.

Setting steel station widths around 0.3-0.4 and depths 0.2-0.24, with surcoat stations slightly larger to sit visibly outside the cuirass, confirming the loft's width/depth convention matches binormal/normal axes correctly. For the neck, I'll lathe a small gorget profile, and for the helm, loft stations around the head bone shape.

Adding a vertical nose-guard bar across the eye slit, then attaching the crimson plume at the helm's crown with a sweeping path of points rising up and back from the top of the head.

Adding rivet details by scattering small gold studs across the pauldrons and cuirass surface for extra texture.

For the finishing touches I'm thinking through the paint functions available—mottle, stripes, paint, cells, grain, gradient—and planning to use a custom paint function for the steel's surface variation.

Defining steel paint...

Defining more palette colors...

For the griffin texture, I'm sketching an SVG silhouette and thinking through how its fill color should work with tinting — since a grayscale drawing gets multiplied by the tint color, a pure black fill would stay black regardless of the silver tint applied, so I need to reconsider the fill value to get the right tinted result.

Still writing griffin paths...

I'm checking that the shield and surcoat can share the same texture, making sure the plane geometry has proper UVs for texture mapping, and handling the tint logic so white is used as a neutral base color when a texture is applied instead of the actual color string.

Now I'm working out placement for the emblems: sizing the surcoat emblem plane and figuring out the shield's front-face position using the part's local coordinate frame, accounting for thickness and normal direction so the emblem sits flush against the shield's front surface with the correct orientation.

Checking the normal direction: with the quat basis (x, y, normal) where normal = x×y = +Z, the front face points outward correctly. For a viewer standing at +Z looking toward -Z in a right-handed system, world +X appears to their right, so I need to work out whether the griffin's orientation on the shield reads correctly from that viewpoint rather than mirrored.

For the surcoat emblem, I'm finding the nearest surface point to a target location, then building a frame by offsetting slightly along the surface normal and orienting the part so its local +Z aligns with that normal while +Y stays roughly world-up. This depends on the surcoat mesh being built first so the nearest-surface lookup works correctly.

I'm also sizing the emblem plane to roughly match the griffin graphic's proportions, and confirming I don't need decals or cards for this. Then I'm reviewing joint creation syntax — root joints have no parent, and I'm checking whether a "spine" role is valid for the hip joint.

I'm defining the head joint parented to the neck, and then building out the spine chain from hips through two spine segments to the neck, specifying positions and names for each joint in sequence.

Adding head joint then starting the arm chains...

Defining the leg chain now, checking ankle height against the foot box so the bottom sits flush with the ground at y=0.

Setting up sweep radii along each limb chain—thigh thicker near hip tapering to narrower at the ankle—to approximate tapered armor plating.

Adding gauntlet spheres at the wrists for both hands, positioned against the bone locations, then placing the sword blade geometry gripped in the right hand.

Adding the crossguard as a small gold box positioned just above the blade start near the wrist, sized to cover the hilt-blade junction. I'm skipping the pommel and letting the gauntlet cover the grip area, then working out the blade's local axis orientation so it spans correctly in width and length.

Now I'm setting up the shield as an extruded kite shape positioned at the left wrist, checking its outline dimensions against the torso width to confirm it sits just outside the body without clipping, and sizing it so the top reaches shoulder height and the bottom point stays near waist level.

I'm working out the shield paint, defining a reusable "dented" helper that uses cell noise to scatter darker battle-damage patches across a base armor color, keeping the function generic so it can take any base color and a seed for variation.

For scratches, I'm considering adding thin cracked-looking lines along cell borders based on how close two distance values are, tuning the threshold so the lines stay fine rather than overwhelming the texture, and estimating pixel width to make sure they read as subtle scratches rather than a dense network.

For the pauldrons, I'm planning a lathe-based shoulder armor piece using a layered dome profile positioned at the shoulder joint, with multiple stacked lathe layers of decreasing radius to build up the rounded form, plus gold trim stripes on top.

Now I'm mirroring the pauldron setup for the right shoulder and confirming segment/smoothing defaults are fine, then moving to the cuirass, which I'll build as a lofted steel shape starting from the chest point.

Adding surcoat loft stations...

Placing the emblem around y~1.0 with surcoat height 0.27, so z lands at 0.135. I'll skip the gold trim and belt details for now to keep things simple.

Now I'm defining the cape as a membrane attached at the spine, with shoulder-level edge points forming the top anchor and a torn, uneven hem below for the bottom edge.

I'm increasing the row count to six for smoother geometry, applying a crimson-to-dark gradient running from the shoulder down to the hem, and then moving on to define the plume's sweep path relative to the head bone.

Writing plume sweep points...

Adding a gorget cylinder at the neck in battered steel, then scattering rivets across the cuirass front using a filtered surface scatter and placing small spheres at each point.

Adding gold trim stripes...

I'll put the trim slightly above the hem, let round caps handle the loft ends, add simple box sabatons for feet, and skip the belt detail. For the legs I'll reuse the chain tube with overlapping radius at the hip joint, then start writing out the actual scene code.

Writing imports and paint helpers...

Defining mottled color palettes...

Now I'm adding gold filigree stripes to the pauldron and starting to build out the griffin SVG path with white fill and gray stroke outlines.

I'm checking that the griffin emblem texture tints properly against the silver material and confirming it won't be mistaken for grey fills. Now I'm working out the local coordinate placement for mounting the emblem on the shield's front face, accounting for thickness and bevel offset.

Next I'm repeating a similar setup for the surcoat emblem, finding the nearest surface point and positioning the plane slightly offset along the surface normal, oriented with an aim quaternion.

Now orthogonalizing Y against the sweep direction so the frame stays properly aligned. For the shield boss, I'm lathing a small steel dome profile positioned at the shield's front center, oriented along the shield's normal axis.

I'm reconsidering placement — the griffin emblem and boss both want to sit at the shield's center, so I'll simplify by centering the griffin design and skipping the boss detail and gold rim border to avoid overlap, applying a battered blue finish to the shield instead.

For the pauldron, I'm defining a lathe profile curving upward into a bowl shape, then building it in layers — stacking three lathe calls at slightly different heights with the same scale, positioned at the shoulder point to create a stepped plate effect.

I'm mirroring this for the right shoulder using negative x, assigning joint weights to shoulderL and shoulderR bones, and tagging the metal with a gold-stripe paint detail. For legs I'm sweeping a greaves profile along the leg chain with a battered steel finish, and for gauntlets I'm considering sphere or box geometry with a paint fill for the knuckle plates.

Now I'm positioning sabatons as box geometry at the ankle bones for each foot, keeping knees simple without kneecap details, and confirming the sweep function works correctly with chain-based bones. For the sword, I'm extruding a blade profile along the wrist bone with beveled edges and a battered steel color, then adding a gold box guard positioned at the hilt to complete the weapon.

Adding grip and pommel...

I'll skip the crest ridges for simplicity. Let me verify the loft signature takes stations and options, making sure color is properly supplied even though it's technically optional in SweepOptions.

Checking the remaining calls: sweep requires color, membrane needs color and thickness, extrude needs color/at/thickness, lathe needs color/at, and stick is used for rivets with embed options. The surface scatter method works synchronously, so I'm now setting up the module exports with meta info and the default knight builder function.

Verifying joint roles and bone references throughout—head, spine, arms, legs all use correct role strings, and helm/pauldron geometry correctly references bone joints like "head" and "shoulderL" as JointRef strings.

Now checking that shield and gauntlet placements align with the wrist joint position, confirming chain name arrays have exactly three entries for arms and legs.

Writing tabard hem geometry...

The hem sweep ending with a rounded cap at the bottom should work fine. For the cuirass and pauldron, I'll apply a battered texture effect to the steel surface and gold stripe base, using consistent random seeds for both.

Now I'm writing the final module, importing the needed helpers from the SDK and setting up the helm slit geometry with a small dark box shape before assembling everything together.

Defining the color palettes...

I'm sketching a bowl-shaped profile curve for the pauldron geometry, confirming the point array type works with the outline input format, then moving into building the pauldron shape itself.

Now I'm lathing the bowl profile at three decreasing scales for each shoulder side, with a battered steel-and-gold striped paint attached to the shoulder joint bones. I'll define FILIGREE as a shared stripe paint instead of recreating it per call, and double-check that the `at` position array and `PointInput` types line up correctly.

Moving on, I'm adding the cape as a membrane between two edges with a crimson-to-dark-red gradient and thin segmented rows attached to the spine bone. Then I'm placing small steel sphere gauntlets at the wrists, boxy steel feet at the ankles (checking the geometry doesn't clip through the leg chain), and sphere knee guards attached to the knee bones, deciding to keep them battered steel rather than gold for consistency before moving on to the gorget.

For the gorget, I'm using a closed cylinder shape at the neck bone to form the collar, plus helm details like eye slits, a nasal guard, and a swept crest ridge running front-to-back along the top of the head for visual flair, with a plume also attached to the head bone. I'm satisfied the code is complete, so I'm doing a final pass checking the loft station format, the sweep radius keying for the legs across three points, and confirming I'll just output the finished code block without extra explanatory text.

Writing final part assembly...
